newsitem.title: USA: Kaiser nurses strike in northern California.
newsitem.headline: Kaiser nurses strike in northern California.

text.p: Thousands of nurses staged a one-day strike at Kaiser Permanente hospitals and clinics in northern California on Wednesday in protest against a management proposal to freeze or cut their basic salaries.
Nurses picketed Kaiser hospitals in several northern California cities and members of several other unions refused to cross picket lines, according to the nurses' union.
Rose Ann DeMoro, executive director of the California Nurses Association, said 7,500 nurses were on strike at 16 Kaiser Permanente hospitals and 29 clinics.

The total on strike, including clerical workers, X-ray technicians and others, could be as high as 26,000, she said, although she said the actual number was difficult to estimate. "I'm overwhelmed with the response. It's phenomenal," DeMoro said.
Kaiser Permanente spokeswoman Lila Petersen had no estimate of how many people were on strike. But she said "a significant number of the other union people have crossed the picket lines."

Kaiser Permanente, the nation's largest health maintenance organization, said it continued operating the hospitals and clinics at a reduced level. Some doctors filled in as nurses, managers trained as nurses did nursing duties and more than 100 nurses were brought up from Kaiser hospitals in southern California, Petersen said.

Some patients had been moved out to other community hospitals in anticipation of the strike and patients with appointments Wednesday were asked to reschedule them. But the hospitals remained open for emergencies.
The inpatient bed occupancy rate at the affected hospitals, which normally averaged 52 percent, dropped to a little over 20 percent, Petersen said.
"It's been very calm. The situation is stable at our facilities. Things are going quite well," she said.

The nurses have worked without a contract since January 30. They struck over proposals by Kaiser to freeze the pay of 60 percent of the 7,500 nurses for four years with a one percent pay rise in the last two years of a six-year contract.
Kaiser proposes to cut the salaries of the other 40 percent of the nurses, mainly in the Sacramento and Santa Rosa areas, by 2.5 percent each year.
All of the nurses could earn raises of up to 2 percent each year under a new performance-based system.
Petersen said the nurses were among the most highly paid in the market, adding: "We are dealing with a very competitive marketplace in terms of for-profit healthcare companies," she said.

Another issue is what the nurses say is declining quality of healthcare in the Kaiser system, an allegation strongly denied by management. "The problem is that they (Kaiser) brought in consultants that are ratcheting down the standard of care," DeMoro of the California Nurses Association said.
DeMoro said she did not rule out more one-day strikes or even a "full-blown" strike if the dispute persists.
